Adult females of the longfin icedevil, Aethotaxis mitopteryx, attain a maximum total length of 33.6 centimeters [Li = 33.6 centimeters], a value derived from extensive benthic trawl surveys in the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Males grow to a considerably larger size, with an ultimate total length recorded at 44.3 centimeters [Li = 44.3 centimeters], a pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism that is uncommon among nototheniid fishes and may reflect divergent selective pressures related to male-male competition for spawning territories. This species exhibits a markedly slow life history, typical of many Antarctic teleosts inhabiting the stable, frigid waters of the continental shelf. The age at which the chorion ruptures and the yolk-sac larva emerges has been determined from laboratory incubation experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]; under these conditions, the embryonic period lasts approximately 95 days [ab = approximately 95 days], a protracted developmental duration that is consistent with the extremely low metabolic rates observed in polar fish embryos. Upon eclosion, the lecithotrophic larva begins absorbing its endogenous yolk reserves, a phase that precedes the onset of first exogenous feeding.

The wet weight of a newly emerged yolk-sac larva is quite minimal, measuring only 0.014 grams [Wwb = 0.014 grams], reflecting the small volume of the fertilized ovum from which it hatched. This neonatal mass is comparable to that reported for other nototheniids with similar egg diameters, such as Trematomus bernacchii, upon which initial estimates were based. As the larva transitions from its endotrophic phase to exogenous nutrition, it embarks on a prolonged period of somatic growth that will eventually culminate in the attainment of sexual maturity. The onset of puberty, marked by the histological differentiation of the gonads and the commencement of gametogenesis, is associated with a threshold total length of 18.3 centimeters [Lp = 18.3 centimeters] in this species. This length at puberty corresponds to a moderate body size relative to the species' ultimate dimensions, suggesting that individuals invest substantially in somatic growth before initiating reproductive development, a life-history strategy that is common among long-lived, slow-maturing marine fishes.

Corresponding to this length at maturity, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at approximately 43 grams [Wwp = approximately 43 grams], a value that aligns with the allometric growth relationship observed in adult Aethotaxis mitopteryx. Once individuals surpass this threshold, they continue to accumulate body mass, eventually reaching a much greater ultimate wet weight. The maximum recorded adult body mass for females, based on asymptotic growth models fitted to length-weight data, is 283 grams [Wwi = 283 grams]. Male longfin icedevils, consistent with their larger ultimate length, achieve a substantially heavier maximum weight, with the largest individuals on record attaining 666.8 grams [Wwi = 666.8 grams]. This pronounced sexual difference in asymptotic mass further underscores the dimorphic growth trajectory between the sexes, a characteristic that likely influences their respective reproductive roles and energy budgets during the spawning season under the stable thermal conditions typical of their habitat.

Reproductive output and its underlying thermal dependency have been investigated through controlled aquarium studies at the New Zealand Antarctic Research Institute. At a constant ambient temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C], females were observed to produce a single clutch containing approximately 8 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 8 eggs per spawning event], with a maximum of roughly one such spawning event each year [F_R_i = roughly one such spawning event each year]. This low fecundity, coupled with the large size of the yolky eggs, is characteristic of a k-selected reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. The protracted developmental period of the embryos, combined with the infrequent reproductive events, contributes to the overall low maximum annual reproductive rate of this species. The same thermal regime of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C] also appears to constrain the upper bounds of these life-history parameters, as metabolic demands remain extremely low, limiting the rate at which females can provision their developing oocytes.

The natural lifespan of Aethotaxis mitopteryx is remarkably extended, with the oldest documented individual recovered from a long-term tagging study estimated to have lived for approximately 36 years [am = approximately 36 years], a longevity that rivals that of certain deep-sea fishes despite the species' occupation of relatively shallo at a temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C]w shelf waters. These data were collected from fish inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C], a frigid environment that slows the aging process and reduces the metabolic costs associated with somatic maintenance over decades. The combination of a late age at puberty, extreme longevity, low fecundity, and large egg size places the longfin icedevil firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among Antarctic notothenioids. This suite of life-history traits makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbation, as any increase in mortality rates due to climate warming or fishing pressure would require an exceptionally long time for the population to recover, given its inherently low maximum rate of increase.
